```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

This vignette reproduces the Python package's Tasmania notebook using the same
bundled rasters and numerical settings. It calculates four indicators:

| Indicator | R call | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Connectedness | `connectedness(..., option = 1)` | Connectivity to condition-weighted habitat in the surrounding landscape |
| Connected habitat | `connectedness(..., option = 3)` | Square root of connectedness multiplied by local habitat condition |
| PARC-connectedness | `connectedness(..., pa_file = ...)` | Connectedness evaluated at protected cells, optionally restricted to protected destinations |
| BERI | `beri(...)` | Bioclimatic Ecosystem Resilience Index using compositional turnover under climate scenarios |

All indicator results stay in memory as georeferenced `terra::SpatRaster` objects
and are plotted directly. No indicator output files or data downloads are needed.

## 1. Read the bundled data

As in blockCV, external raster files are shipped in `inst/extdata` and located
with base R's `system.file()`. There is no separate data-reading helper.
These paths work from any working directory after package installation.

```{r inputs}
library(connectivity)
library(terra)

condition_file <- system.file("extdata", "site_condition.tif",
                              package = "connectivity", mustWork = TRUE)
pa_file <- system.file("extdata", "pa_proportion.tif",
                       package = "connectivity", mustWork = TRUE)
climate_dir <- system.file("extdata", "transgrids",
                           package = "connectivity", mustWork = TRUE)

condition <- rast(condition_file)
pa <- rast(pa_file)
condition
global(condition, c("min", "max"), na.rm = TRUE)
global(pa, c("min", "max", "mean"), na.rm = TRUE)
```

The rasters cover Tasmania, Australia on a common grid: 588 columns by 516 rows,
EPSG:4326, at 30 arc-second resolution (approximately 1 km). Habitat condition
and protected-area proportions range from zero to one; missing cells are `NA`.
Auxiliary rasters must share the condition raster's CRS, resolution and pixel
grid and cover the analysis window. They are not resampled automatically.

```{r input-maps, fig.width=9, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Bundled habitat condition and protected-area proportions."}
plot(c(condition, pa), main = c("Habitat condition", "Protected fraction"),
     col = hcl.colors(100, "viridis"), range = c(0, 1))
```

## 2. Choose resolution levels

The Rust engine builds its aggregation pyramid internally. No precomputed
GeoTIFF overviews are required. The table below mirrors the Python notebook's
resolution planning using ordinary R calculations. Dimensions round up at each
aggregation level. The search span in coordinate units is
`outer_window * level * resolution`; here those units are degrees, with physical
east-west distances varying by latitude.

```{r resolution-planning}
candidate_levels <- 2^(0:9)
resolution_plan <- data.frame(
    level = candidate_levels,
    columns = ceiling(ncol(condition) / candidate_levels),
    rows = ceiling(nrow(condition) / candidate_levels),
    resolution_degrees = res(condition)[1] * candidate_levels,
    search_span_degrees = 7 * candidate_levels * max(res(condition))
)
resolution_plan$cells <- with(resolution_plan, columns * rows)
resolution_plan$percent_base <- 100 * resolution_plan$cells / ncell(condition)
resolution_plan$note <- ifelse(
    pmin(resolution_plan$columns, resolution_plan$rows) < 16,
    "Small grid: review", ""
)
knitr::kable(resolution_plan, digits = 3)
```

Levels through 32 retain at least 16 cells in each dimension for this grid;
coarser levels deserve review. The examples use `levels = c(2, 4, 8, 16, 32)`;
level 1 is always included by the engine. `lambdas` specifies dispersal
bandwidths in kilometres. `n_threads = NULL` uses the engine's default worker
count. All calls below use the same settings as the Python notebook.

## 3. Connectedness

`option = 1` returns raw connectedness, describing how well each cell is linked
to condition-weighted habitat in its surrounding landscape.

```{r connectedness}
conns <- connectedness(
    condition_file = condition,
    lambdas = c(2, 20, 50),
    max_cost = 2,
    window_size = 5,
    outer_window = 7,
    levels = c(2, 4, 8, 16, 32),
    option = 1,
    window_mode = "circular",
    n_threads = NULL
)
plot(conns, main = "Connectedness", col = hcl.colors(100, "BrBG"),
     range = c(0, 0.8))
```

## 4. Connected habitat

`option = 3` (the default) calculates `sqrt(connectedness * condition)`, so local
habitat condition also affects the score. `option = 2` would return the product
without the square root.

```{r connected-habitat}
connhabitat <- connectedness(
    condition_file = condition,
    lambdas = c(2, 20, 50),
    max_cost = 2,
    window_size = 5,
    outer_window = 7,
    levels = c(2, 4, 8, 16, 32),
    option = 3,
    window_mode = "circular",
    n_threads = NULL
)
plot(connhabitat, main = "Connected habitat", col = hcl.colors(100, "BrBG"),
     range = c(0, 0.8))
```

## 5. PARC-connectedness

Supplying `pa_file` calculates protected-area connectedness. The condition used
for habitat and traversal is the maximum of habitat condition and protected
fraction, and only cells with a positive protected fraction receive scores.
With `pa_to_pa = FALSE`, destinations may include the surrounding unprotected
landscape. Set `pa_to_pa = TRUE` to restrict destinations to protected cells,
weighted by protected fraction at coarser levels. PARC returns raw
connectedness regardless of `option`.

```{r parc}
parc <- connectedness(
    condition_file = condition,
    pa_file = pa,
    pa_to_pa = FALSE,
    lambdas = c(2, 20, 50),
    max_cost = 2,
    window_size = 5,
    outer_window = 7,
    levels = c(2, 4, 8, 16, 32),
    window_mode = "circular",
    n_threads = NULL
)
plot(parc, main = "PARC-connectedness", col = hcl.colors(100, "viridis"),
     range = c(0, 1))
```

## 6. BERI

BERI combines habitat connectedness with compositional turnover under climate
scenarios. Each climate file contains 19 bands in matching order. `1990.tif`
is the current baseline; the six other files are future scenarios. Scenario
identifiers below are the original filenames.

```{r climate-inputs}
current_file <- file.path(climate_dir, "1990.tif")
scenario_names <- c(
    "ACC50_85", "GFD50_85", "IPS50_26",
    "IPS50_45", "IPS50_60", "IPS50_85"
)
future_files <- file.path(climate_dir, paste0(scenario_names, ".tif"))
basename(future_files)
current_climate <- rast(current_file)
nlyr(current_climate)
compareGeom(condition, current_climate, lyrs = FALSE)
```

The climate grids share the condition grid, so the resolution plan above also
applies to them. Pass the current baseline first and future scenarios in the
order shown. The result is one BERI raster combining these scenarios, without
the Connected Habitat condition multiplication or square-root transformation.
Omitting `future_files` calculates the current-climate index only.

```{r beri}
beri_map <- beri(
    condition_file = condition,
    current_file = current_file,
    future_files = future_files,
    lambdas = c(2, 20, 50),
    max_cost = 2,
    window_size = 5,
    outer_window = 7,
    levels = c(2, 4, 8, 16, 32),
    window_mode = "circular",
    n_threads = NULL
)
plot(beri_map, main = "BERI", col = hcl.colors(100, "RdYlGn"),
     range = c(0, 0.8))
```

## 7. Compare all indicators

The five panels show the input habitat condition and four indicator results,
cropped to the Tasmanian mainland for display. Calculations above use the
complete bundled landscape. Display ranges match the Python comparison:
zero to one for the first four panels and zero to 0.8 for BERI.

```{r comparison, fig.width=10, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Habitat condition and the four connectivity indicators on the Tasmanian mainland."}
mainland <- ext(144.4, 148.6, -43.7, -40.6)
maps <- list(condition, conns, connhabitat, parc, beri_map)
titles <- c("(a) Habitat condition", "(b) Connectedness", "(c) Connected habitat",
            "(d) PARC-connectedness", "(e) BERI")
palettes <- list(
    hcl.colors(100, "BrBG"), hcl.colors(100, "BrBG"), hcl.colors(100, "BrBG"),
    hcl.colors(100, "viridis"), hcl.colors(100, "RdYlGn")
)
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(3, 3, 3, 4))
for (i in seq_along(maps)) {
    plot(crop(maps[[i]], mainland), main = titles[i], col = palettes[[i]],
       range = c(0, if (i == 5) 0.8 else 1))
}
plot.new()
par(old_par)
```

## Data sources and licence

The nine GeoTIFFs are unchanged copies of the Python package's example data.
They are distributed under **CC BY-NC-SA 4.0**, separately from the package's
MIT-licensed code. The installed data README records the grid, layer metadata,
attribution and licence:

```{r data-documentation, eval=FALSE}
file.show(system.file("extdata", "README.md", package = "connectivity",
                      mustWork = TRUE))
```
